Alcmene.note: Jupiter assumes Amphitryon’s identity, prolongs the night, and fathers Hercules.
Jupiter deceives Alcmene by appropriating her husband’s appearance.

Alexiares.note: Later Greek sources name Alexiares as a son of Heracles and Hebe.

Allecto.note: Juno summons Allecto to infect Amata and Turnus with war-fury.

Amalthea.note: Ops entrusts the infant Jupiter to Amalthea, whose goat nurses him.

Ampelus.note: Nonnus presents the youth Ampelus as Bacchus's beloved.
After Ampelus dies, he is transformed into the vine associated with Bacchus.

Amphitryon.note: Amphitryon is Hercules’ social father, though Jupiter is his biological father.

Amycus.note: Pollux defeats Amycus in a boxing contest during the Argonautic voyage.

Amykos.note: The disputed Luna-like figure Losna witnesses Amykos competing against Pollux.

Anchises.note: The serpent may be Genius loci or Anchises' attendant; Virgil leaves it unresolved.
Anchises physically carries them because battle-polluted Aeneas will not touch sacred objects.
Disguised as a maiden, Venus sleeps with Anchises and foretells Aeneas's birth.
Anchises is Venus's mortal Trojan lover and Aeneas's father.

Anicetus.note: Later Greek sources name Anicetus as a son of Heracles and Hebe.

Anna Perenna.note: Anna veils herself as Minerva and tricks Mars into unveiling her.
Anna claims to mediate Mars's suit for Minerva, then substitutes herself as the veiled bride.

Annona.note: Annona holds a statuette of Concordia, linking grain supply with social stability.

Antaeus.note: Hercules defeats Antaeus by lifting him away from his sustaining mother Earth.

Anteros.note: Cicero identifies his third Cupid with Anteros.
One learned genealogical scheme makes Mars and Venus parents of Anteros.

Antinous.note: The deified Antinous is portrayed with Silvanus' rustic and vegetative attributes.

Antiope.note: Jupiter takes a satyr’s form for his union with Antiope.

Aollius.note: Plutarch preserves a disputed tradition making Aollius or Avillius Romulus’s son.

Arachne.note: Arachne challenges Minerva to weave; Minerva cannot fault her rival's craftsmanship.
Minerva destroys Arachne's faultless tapestry and strikes her after the contest.
Minerva prevents Arachne's final death and transforms her into a perpetually spinning spider.

Aradia.note: Leland's Diana bears Aradia as her daughter by Lucifer.
Diana sends Aradia to teach witchcraft and resistance among the oppressed.

Arcas.note: Jupiter fathers Arcas with Callisto in Hellenized tradition.

Arethusa.note: Arethusa tells Ceres that Proserpina has become queen below.
Arethusa tells Ceres that she saw Proserpina ruling in the underworld.

Argonauts.note: Castor and Pollux voyage as members of the Argonauts.

Argus.note: Disguised as a shepherd, Mercury charms Argus with music and narrative and induces sleep.
Mercury decapitates the sleeping hundred-eyed guardian, earning the epithet Argicida.

Arruns.note: Diana orders Opis to kill Arruns for slaying Camilla.

Arsinoe.note: A rival Messenian genealogy names Arsinoe rather than Coronis as his mother.

Arsippus.note: Cicero's third Aesculapius is a son of Arsippus and Arsinoe.

Ascalaphus.note: Ascalaphus reports Proserpina's eating, preventing her complete release from Pluto's realm.
After he reports her eating seeds, Proserpina transforms him into an owl.

Ascanius.note: Cupid assumes Ascanius’s appearance while the real boy is put to sleep and removed.
When Ascanius transferred them to Alba Longa, they miraculously returned to Lavinium.

Atalanta.note: Venus causes or permits Atalanta's transformation into a lion after the couple's sacrilege.

Athamas.note: Juno commissions the destruction of Athamas and Ino through madness.
Ino is the wife of Athamas in the inherited Greek genealogy.

Attis.note: Bellona's Ostian sanctuary occupied Magna Mater's campus alongside Attis's shrine.
Cybele loves Attis and bears his child before her father kills him.
Some traditions describe Attis as Cybele's child or son.
After Attis sleeps with Sagaritis, Cybele's vengeance precipitates his madness and castration.
Cybele chooses Attis as permanent guardian and requires him to remain chaste.
Cybele releases a lion to frighten the repentant Attis back into her wilderness.
After Cybele's lion drives him back, Attis remains her permanent servant.
The Mother and Agdistis seek preservation of dead Attis rather than full resurrection.
The Mother gathers and buries Attis's severed parts; violets arise from his blood.
Flora includes Attis among wounded or dead youths preserved through flowers.
An inscription identifies Attis as the Genius of the dendrophori association.
Luna appears in the cosmic frame surrounding Attis and Cybele.
Silvanus' Dendrophorus title and tree-bearing role overlap with organizations connected to Attis.
Macrobius interprets Attis as the sun or a solar power.

Augustus.myth: Provincial joint cult of Roma and Augustus
Augustus.note: Augustus authorized provincial temples joining his worship with Roma's.
Roma sits beside the Jupiter-like enthroned Augustus as an equal imperial power.
Provincial coin types depict Roma crowning Augustus while holding a cornucopia.

Aura.note: Aura belongs to a late Dionysiac erotic cycle centered on Dionysus.

Auruncus.note: Gellius lists Auruncus alongside Robigus as powers placated to avert harm.

Belatucadrus.note: Northern British worshippers equated Belatucadrus with Mars.

Belisama.note: A sparsely attested Gallic composite name identifies Minerva with Belisama.

Bia.note: Victoria is called her sister only through identification with Nike.
Bia.date: late eighth or early seventh century BCE

Bona Dea.myth: Exclusion from Bona Dea’s women-only sanctuary
Bona Dea.note: Denied water, Hercules forces entry and retaliates by excluding women from his altar.
Disputed imperial imagery has been interpreted as Bona Dea crowning Vulcan.

Braciaca.note: A Bakewell inscription identifies the obscure god Braciaca with Mars.

Brontes.note: Brontes labors under Vulcan on thunderbolts, Mars's chariot, and Minerva's aegis.

Bull.myth: Pursuit, capture, and transport of the bull
Bull.note: Mithras pursues, seizes, rides, drags, and carries the bull toward the cave.
Mithras subdues the bull and kills it with a dagger.

Caca.note: A poorly attested tradition makes Caca betray her brother to Hercules.

Cacus.note: Hercules discovers the stolen cattle and kills Cacus.

Cacus.myth: Battle with the fire-breathing cave monster
Cacus.note: Hercules tears open Cacus’ cave and strangles Vulcan’s monstrous son.
In a rationalized variant, Hercules defeats the barbarian chieftain Cacus in war.
Virgil calls the fire-breathing monster Cacus a son of Vulcan.

Cadmus.note: In the transferred Greek genealogy, Ino-Matuta is Cadmus' daughter.

Caeculus.myth: Caeculus conceived through a hearth spark
Caeculus.note: Vulcan impregnates Caeculus's mother through a spark from the hearth.

Caelus.note: One learned genealogy makes a distinct Mercury the son of Caelus.
Arnobius' polemical catalogue includes a Mercury born from the highest Heaven.
Caelus appears as a cosmic figure framing Mithraic compositions without a narrated encounter.
Cicero's first of four Vulcans is a son of Caelus.

Caenis.note: Neptune rapes Caenis on the shore and afterward offers a wish.
Neptune transforms Caenis into the invulnerable male warrior Caeneus.

Calliope.note: Calliope is named as adjudicating Proserpina's dispute with Venus.

Callisto.note: Diana expels Callisto from her virgin company after discovering her pregnancy.
One version makes Juno transform Jupiter’s pregnant lover Callisto.
Juno persecutes Callisto, though sources disagree about who transforms her.
Jupiter assumes Diana’s form and sexually assaults or seduces Callisto.
Jupiter deceives Callisto by taking the appearance of Diana.

Calumny.note: Truth approaches behind Calumny's procession as its compositional and moral opposite.

Camenae.myth: Numa’s consultations in the sacred spring-grove
Camenae.note: Egeria was dear to the Camenae and shared their consecrated grove.

Camese.note: Janus and Camese share sovereignty in an antiquarian account.
Some later genealogies interpret Janus and Camese as siblings.
Some later genealogies interpret Camese as Janus’s spouse.

Camilla.note: Diana patronizes the dedicated virgin warrior and orders vengeance after her death.

Campestres.note: Dacian dedications join Silvanus and the Silvanae with protectors of open ground and cavalry exercise.

Camulus.note: Roman interpretation identified the indigenous god Camulus with Mars.

Canace.note: Arachne’s tapestry depicts Neptune assuming bull form for Canace.

Canens.note: A late variant names Canens as the daughter of Janus and Venilia.
Picus is Canens’s faithful husband; his disappearance causes her fatal wandering.

Canis.myth: Celestial Dog explains the canine sacrifice
Canis.note: Ovid connects Robigo’s canine victim with the grain-threatening celestial Dog.

Capaneus.note: Capaneus is one variant candidate for the dead person Aesculapius restored.

Carna.note: Janus defeats the nymph’s evasive trick and sexually coerces her.
Janus grants her authority over hinges and a protective white-thorn branch.

Castor and Pollux.note: Their temple and Concordia’s were dedicated together within Tiberius’s dynastic program.
Variant Hellenized genealogies include the Dioscuri among Jupiter’s children.

Cautes.note: Cautes accompanies Mithras beside the bull-killing scene with an upraised torch.
Cautes sometimes attends Mithras as the god emerges fully formed from rock.

Cautopates.note: Cautopates accompanies Mithras beside the bull-killing scene with a lowered torch.
Cautopates sometimes attends Mithras as the god emerges fully formed from rock.

Cephalus.note: Cephalus is an abducted lover of Eos and father of Phaethon in one genealogy.
Aurora carries the unwilling newlywed Cephalus away and later releases him.
Angered by his devotion to Procris, Aurora induces Cephalus to test his wife's fidelity.

Chione.note: Diana kills Chione with an arrow after Chione boasts of surpassing her beauty.

Chloris.myth: Flora reveals her former Greek identity
Chloris.note: Flora says she was formerly the Greek nymph Chloris.

Christ.note: Christian writers apply solar language to Christ but provide no cultic equation with Sol Invictus.
Christ.source: Christian homilies; Chronography of 354; Leo I

Chrysaor.note: Chrysaor is Neptune’s child through Medusa in transferred Greek genealogy.

Cleitus.note: Eos abducts the beautiful Cleitus and places him among the immortals.

Clytemnestra.note: Clytemnestra is their sister or half-sister in competing genealogies.

Clytie.note: Sol abandons the jealous Clytie, who wastes away watching him and becomes a heliotropic flower.

Cocidius.note: Provincial inscriptions could identify Cocidius as a body's or locality's Genius and protector.
Northern British dedications identify the indigenous god Cocidius with Mars.
Romano-British dedications explicitly or functionally equate Silvanus with Cocidius.

Condatis.note: The confluence-associated god Condatis was worshipped as Mars Condatis.

Conspiracy.note: Truth approaches the allegorical scene in opposition to Conspiracy attending Calumny.

Constantinopolis.note: Coinage and art pair Roma with Constantinopolis as distinct imperial capital-personifications.

Coronis.note: Coronis is Aesculapius' mother in the dominant Pindaric and Epidaurian genealogies.
Coronis receives Roman calendrical cult beside her son on 1 January.
A fragmentary calendar jointly lists Coronis, Aesculapius, and Vediovis.

Corybantes.note: Their armed dancing, shield-clashing, and music accompany the rites of Mother-Rhea.

Credulitas.note: Credulitas resides among the personified forces inside Fama's cosmic house.

Creusa.note: A late Hellenizing pedigree makes Janus a child of Creusa.

Crocus.note: Flora claims Crocus among wounded youths rendered beautiful as flowers.

Cronus.note: As Rhea, Cybele is the consort of Cronus.
Roman interpretatio equates Saturn with the Greek Titan Cronus.

Culśanś.note: Modern scholarship compares Janus with the Etruscan two-faced gate deity.

Curetes.note: Through her Rhea identity, Ops benefits from their weapon-clashing concealment of Jupiter.

Cyane.note: Cyane attempts unsuccessfully to stop Pluto and save Proserpina.

Daphne.note: Cupid shoots Daphne with a leaden arrow that imposes aversion to Apollo.

Dardanus.note: Learned tradition made Dardanus carry their divine predecessors from Samothrace to Troy.

Day.note: Cicero's learned catalogue makes one Venus the daughter of Day and Caelus.

Dea Dia.note: Invoked during Dea Dia's rites to preserve her agricultural domain.

Deianira.myth: Marriage after the contest with Achelous
Deianira.note: Hercules wins Deianira after defeating her river-god suitor Achelous.

Deiopea.note: Juno promises Deiopea in marriage to Aeolus as payment for the storm.

Deucalion and Pyrrha.note: Jupiter ends the flood and permits the surviving pair to restore humanity.

Deverra.note: Deverra's broom-sign completes the threshold defense against Silvanus.

Di Indigetes.note: The Di Indigetes and Bellona are jointly invoked in the devotio prayer.
The Di Indigetes and Manes are jointly invoked in Decius’s prayer.

Di Novensiles.note: The Di Novensiles and Bellona are jointly invoked in the devotio prayer.

Dido.note: Disguised as Ascanius, Cupid secretly implants Dido’s passion for Aeneas.

Dies.note: One Mercury in Cicero's learned catalogue is born of Caelus and Dies.

Dike.note: Pax becomes Dike’s sister only through identification with Eirene.

Dione.note: The Homeric genealogy makes Venus or Aphrodite the daughter of Dione and Jupiter.

Discordia.note: Discord advances while Bellona follows wielding a blood-stained scourge.

Dius Fidius.note: They overlap functionally as guarantors of oaths, without attested meeting or fusion.
Dumézil structurally opposed bright, juridical Dius Fidius to dark Summanus; no ancient interaction is attested.

Divi Novensiles.note: The Divi Novensiles and Manes are jointly invoked in Decius’s prayer.

Divus Julius.note: The Senate reportedly titled Caesar Liberator and voted a public temple of Liberty.

Divus Julius.myth: Authorized eastern cult of Roma and Divus Julius
Divus Julius.note: Roman citizens in eastern provinces were permitted to honor Roma with Divus Julius.

Dolichenus.note: Jupiter Dolichenus combines Jupiter with the storm god worshipped at Doliche.

Dolus.note: Dolus secretly copies Veritas but lacks enough clay to give his counterfeit feet.
Dolus.source: Phaedrus, Appendix Perottina, Prometheus et Dolus

Dryads.note: Virgil jointly invokes the Fauns and Dryads as countryside divinities.

Echo.note: Juno restricts Echo’s speech because Echo distracted her during Jupiter’s affairs.

Eirene.note: Roman Pax was translated and represented through the older Greek goddess Eirene.

Elagabal.note: The Emesene god was officially styled Deus Sol Invictus Elagabalus under the emperor Elagabalus.

Elpis.note: Sophocles lyrically calls Greek Phēmē the immortal child of golden Hope.
Greek writers and Roman authors equate Elpis with Spes through translation and interpretatio.

Emathion.note: Emathion is the son of Eos and Tithonus.

Enceladus.note: Virgil names Enceladus as Fama's brother without narrating an encounter.
Some variants associate Minerva with the attack or victory against Enceladus.

Endymion.myth: Luna visits the beautiful sleeper at Latmos
Endymion.note: Luna loves and repeatedly visits the eternally sleeping Endymion.

Enipeus.note: Neptune assumes the river-god Enipeus’s appearance to deceive Tyro.

Envy.note: Truth approaches the allegorical scene in opposition to Envy and Calumny's attendants.

Enyalius.note: Dionysius reports a Greek interpretive equation between Quirinus and Enyalius.

Epione.note: Epione is the usual consort in the expanded healing-family genealogy.

Erichthonius.note: Minerva hides, nurses, and raises the serpent-legged Erichthonius as foster-mother.

Eros.note: Cupid was routinely identified with Greek Eros in Roman literature and art.

Error.note: Error resides among the personified forces inside Fama's cosmic house.

Erulus.note: Feronia is the mother of Erulus, king of Praeneste.
Feronia grants Erulus three lives and three sets of arms.

Esplace.note: Esplace is the Etruscan reception and representation of the healing god.

Eunomia.note: Pax becomes Eunomia’s sister only through identification with Eirene.

Eurydice.note: Proserpina releases Eurydice under a condition that Orpheus later breaks.

Euryphaessa.note: The Homeric Hymn gives Euryphaessa as Selene's mother.

Evander.note: Carmenta is consistently identified as Evander’s mother in the developed legend.

Evander.myth: Evander’s exile and migration to Latium
Evander.note: She counsels Evander, shares his exile, guides him to Latium, and predicts his future.
The Arcadian hero supposedly established her Palatine sanctuary before the Trojan War.

Fate.note: Juno delays but cannot abolish Fate’s decree concerning Rome.
Jupiter administers fate in epic and Stoic theology but cannot consistently override it.
Fate grants Roma lasting, unshaken sovereignty over nations.
Venus cannot wholly reverse mortal fate for Adonis, Aeneas, or Aeneas's companions.

Fates.note: The Fates appear within Dis's infernal administration and alongside him epigraphically.

Fauna.note: Some late traditions make Fauna the wife of Faunus.
Some late traditions make Fauna the sister of Faunus.
Macrobius and related traditions make Fauna Faunus's daughter.
Fauna is sometimes systematized as Faunus's female equivalent.
Faunus desires, beats, intoxicates, and assaults Fauna after becoming a serpent.

Felicitas.note: Imperial programs associated future hope with the divine personification of prosperity.

Fisus Sancius.note: Umbrian oath ritual and hand-covering parallel Fides without establishing identity.

Fontus.note: Janus is named as Fontus’s father by Juturna.

Fortuna Equestris.note: Fortuna Equestris and Vertumnus share a calendrical commemoration date.

Fortuna Primigenia.note: Both goddesses received Roman observances on November 13.

Fortuna Virilis.note: Venus and Fortuna Virilis share April rites whose division of functions ancient sources dispute.

Fraud.note: Truth approaches the allegorical scene in opposition to Fraud attending Calumny.

Furies.note: Jupiter’s Dira ends resistance after Jupiter and Juno reach their settlement.

Furor.note: Furor adorns Mars's crest while Fama flies before the war-chariot.

Galanthis.note: Juno changes Galanthis into a weasel for tricking the birth-goddess.
Galanthis falsely announces the birth, tricking Lucina into releasing her binding posture.
Lucina seizes Galanthis and transforms her into a weasel.

Genita Mana.note: Modern scholars conjecturally identify this death-associated domestic goddess with Mania.

Genitalis.note: Horace offers Genitalis as another name for Ilithyia or Lucina.

Genius Augusti.note: The Genius Augusti stood between two neighborhood Lares in civic cult.

Genius Iovialis.note: Caesius named the Jovial Genius as one of the Penates.

Glauce.note: Cicero's third Diana is daughter of Glauce and Upis.

Hector.myth: Hector entrusts Troy’s Penates to Aeneas
Hector.note: Hector orders Aeneas to save the Penates and seek new walls.

Helen.note: Helen is the twins' sister in genealogical tradition.
The brothers recover Helen after Theseus abducts her.
Variant accounts make Jupiter Helen’s father through the Leda episode.
Venus promises Helen to Paris as the inducement for awarding her the apple.

Hercle.note: Etruscan Hercle was closely equated with Roman Hercules despite distinctive local mythology.

Hercules.myth: Prophecy of Hercules’ arrival in Latium
Hercules.note: Carmenta prophetically anticipates events connected with Hercules’ future arrival in Latium.
Hercules stands at the approach to Concordia’s temple on architectural coins.
Faunus enters Hercules's bed by mistake, and Hercules throws him down.
Hercules petitions Fides, who strengthens Saguntum despite fate forbidding rescue.
Jupiter fathers Hercules with Alcmene in Roman literary tradition.
Jupiter receives and protects his son within the divine order after apotheosis.
Lucina magically prevents Hercules's delivery until Galanthis breaks the obstruction.
Ino's Italian arrival produces a hostile encounter near Hercules' altar before reconciliation.
Hercules enters Pluto's underworld and carries away its guardian Cerberus.
Hercules substitutes modeled heads or lights for offerings allegedly demanded by Dis.
A dedication to Hercules follows the same cultic rules as an altar of Salus.
Hercules reforms offerings to Saturn by substituting candles for alleged human victims.
Macrobius interprets Hercules as the sun or a solar power.
Victoria and Hercules occur within one provincial military dedication.

Hercules Victor.note: Hercules Victor and Vertumnus share a calendrical commemoration date.

Herentas.note: The Campanian desire-goddess Herentas was assimilated to Aphrodite and Venus.

Hermes Trismegistus.note: Mercurius became the Latin designation of the syncretistic Hermes–Thoth revealer.

Herodias.note: Medieval canonistic tradition treats Diana and Herodias as alternative or associated night-ride leaders.

Herse.note: Later Greek tradition makes Selene mother of Herse by Zeus.

Hersilia.note: Quirinus receives his ascended wife, thereafter worshipped beside him as Hora.
Quirinus transforms Hersilia’s body and gives her the divine name Hora.

Hilaira.note: One twin abducts and marries Hilaira during the Leucippid conflict.
The twins seize Hilaira despite her prior association with Idas and Lynceus.

Hippolytus.note: Aesculapius restores the dead Hippolytus, who later becomes Virbius in Italy.
Diana favors his revival, hides him at Aricia, and renames him Virbius.
Venus punishes Hippolytus for chastity and devotion to Diana by causing Phaedra's passion.

Hippomenes.note: Venus gives Hippomenes three golden apples enabling him to defeat Atalanta.
After Hippomenes neglects gratitude, Venus causes or permits his transformation into a lion.

Holy Guardian Angel.note: Modern esoteric systems fuse the Genius with the Holy Guardian Angel or higher self.

Homonoia.note: Greek civic Homonoia is Concordia’s closest functional and political translation.

Hyacinthus.myth: Hyacinthus becomes a flower from blood
Hyacinthus.note: Flora claims to make a flower from Hyacinthus's blood.

Hygieia.note: Hygieia, goddess of health and preservation, is his daughter.
Hygieia regularly appears beside Aesculapius in dedications, associations, and art.
Greek translation and serpent-feeding imagery gradually identified Salus with Hygieia.

Hymen.note: Hymen is associated with Venus and marriage but is not consistently her child.

Hymenaeus.note: Hymenaeus is one variant candidate for the dead person Aesculapius restored.
Late genealogical traditions occasionally make Hymenaeus a child of Dionysus.

Iacchus.note: Roman poets and commentators assimilated the Eleusinian Iacchus to Bacchus or Liber.

Iaso.note: Iaso, goddess of healing or recovery, belongs among his daughters.

Idas.note: The twins fight Idas in the feud following the Leucippid seizure.

Ignorance.note: Truth approaches the allegorical scene opposing the deception encouraged by Ignorance.

Ino.note: Aurora is indirectly linked to Ino through the learned Ino-Leucothea-Mater Matuta equation.
Ino nurses and shelters the infant Bacchus before Juno's persecution.
Juno sends infernal madness against Ino’s household for sheltering Bacchus.

Ino.myth: Ino becomes Leucothea and is identified as Roman Matuta
Ino.note: The deified Ino-Leucothea is identified with Mater Matuta.
Neptune transforms Ino into a sea-divinity after Venus intercedes.

Intercidona.note: Intercidona's axe-sign helps bar threatening Silvanus from the postpartum house.

Inuus.note: Later sources fold Pan's Roman name Inuus into Faunus.
Late commentators merge or coordinate Silvanus with Inuus.

Io.note: Ovid presents the restored Io as worshipped under the identity of Isis.
Juno confines transformed Io under Argus and persecutes her with a gadfly.
Juno eventually permits Io’s restoration after Jupiter promises to stop pursuing her.
Jupiter pursues Io and conceals their encounter with cloud or darkness.
Jupiter changes Io into a cow and surrenders her to Juno.
Mercury frees Io from Argus' guardianship by lulling and killing her watcher.

Iphicles.note: Iphicles is Hercules’ mortal twin or half-brother.

Iphigenia.note: Iphigenia escapes Tauris with Orestes and brings Artemis' image toward Italy.

Iphis.note: Isis changes Iphis's sex so the planned marriage can proceed.

Ira.note: Ira appears alongside Fama in the personified retinue of Mars.

Juno Lucina.note: Interpretive traditions connect their overlapping associations with birth and successful passage into life.

Juno Quiritis.note: Her spear and title are compared with Quirinus to explain his name.

Juno Regina.note: Salus's annual vow was formulated by reference to the vow made to Juno.

Jupiter Anxur.note: Jupiter rules the fields while Feronia rejoices in her nearby grove.

Jupiter Dolichenus.note: Imperial military dedications sometimes pair Juno Regina with Jupiter Dolichenus as consort.

Jupiter Heliopolitanus.note: Venus Heliopolitana appears with Jupiter Heliopolitanus in a local imperial triad.

Jupiter Liber.note: Inscriptions partially fuse Jupiter and Liber, though the precise theology remains disputed.

Jupiter Optimus Maximus.note: Arval records place Salus Publica after Jupiter in annual vows for emperor and state.

Jupiter/Jove.note: Edmund Curll invokes Jove and Cloacina together during Pope's mock-heroic contest.

Justice.note: Fides is poetically presented as the sister of Justice.

Justitia.note: Modern summaries incorrectly name Justitia as Pax’s mother.

Juturna.note: Ovid commemorates both goddesses on 11 January, without describing an interaction or shared rite.
The twins wash and water their horses at Juturna's spring.
Janus fathers Fontus with the fountain goddess Juturna.
Juno authorizes Juturna to delay Turnus’ death and break the truce.

Kratos.note: Victoria is called his sister only through identification with Nike.
Kratos.date: late eighth or early seventh century BCE

Laetitia.note: Laetitia resides among the personified forces inside Fama's cosmic house.

Lar familiaris.note: Granius Flaccus and other authorities reportedly identified Genius with Lar.
In Apuleius's system, a good embodied spirit becomes a household-tending Lar after death.

Lara.myth: Lara's punishment and the Lares' birth
Lara.note: The silenced nymph Lara bears the twin Lares after Mercury assaults her.
Scholarly harmonization sometimes equates Ovid's alternative mother of the Lares with Mania.

Lara.myth: Lara and the birth of the Lares
Lara.note: While escorting the mutilated nymph underground, Mercury rapes her; she later bears the Lares.

Laran.note: The armed Etruscan war god Laran is treated as Mars’s functional counterpart.

Lares Augusti.note: Two Lares Augusti and the leader's Genius formed three neighborhood divinities.

Larunda.note: Scholars have conjecturally amalgamated this Italic or Sabine divinity with Mania.
Varro co-lists their altars among those supposedly vowed by Titus Tatius.

Larva.note: In Apuleius's system, a harmful postmortem spirit becomes a wandering Larva.

Larvae.note: Apuleius contrasts harmful Larvae with Manes whose moral character is uncertain.

Latinus.note: Virgil identifies Latinus as Faunus's son.
Faunus warns Latinus against marrying Lavinia to a Latin suitor.
Virgil gives Latinus solar ancestry through Sol's daughter Circe.

Latona.note: When Lucina means Diana, she inherits Diana's genealogy as Latona's daughter.
North-African evidence pairs Saturn with Latona in a locally reorganized divine configuration.

Learchus.note: Ino is Learchus' mother in the inherited Greek genealogy.
Through identification with Melicertes, Portunus inherits Learchus as his brother.

Leda.note: Leda bears Castor and Pollux in the dominant genealogy.
Jupiter takes a swan’s form in the inherited story of Leda.

Lemures.note: Ovid calls the expelled spirits both Lemures and paternal Manes.
Apuleius makes lemur the general postmortem soul-category encompassing differentiated dead spirits.

Lenus.note: The Treveran healing and tribal god Lenus was worshipped as Mars Lenus.

Leucothoe.note: Desiring Leucothoe, Sol assumes her mother's appearance, enters her chamber, and reveals his radiance.
Unable to revive the buried Leucothoe, Sol transforms her body into frankincense.

Liber.note: Macrobius interprets Liber as the sun or a solar power.

Libera.note: Cicero presents Liber and Libera together as children of Ceres.
Libera is Liber's complementary female cult partner in Roman generative religion.
Cicero's theological explanation calls Libera a child of Ceres.
Ceres and Libera receive joint cult with Liber at the Aventine temple.
Romans identified the older Aventine goddess Libera with Proserpina.

Loucetius.note: Roman provincial worship identified the lightning-associated Loucetius with Mars.

Lua.note: Commanders could dedicate captured enemy weapons to Mars, Bellona, or Lua.

Lua Saturni.note: Lua’s name marks cultic possession or association with Saturn; no meeting survives.

Lupercus.note: Late sources identify Lupercus with Faunus or treat it as his epithet.

Lycurgus.note: Lycurgus is one variant candidate for the dead person Aesculapius restored.

Lynceus.note: The twins fight Lynceus after seizing Phoebe and Hilaira.
Lynceus kills Castor during the Leucippid conflict.
Pollux kills Lynceus after Lynceus kills Castor.

Machaon.note: Machaon, the surgeon and Trojan War physician, is his son.
Later cult images and dedications sometimes group Machaon with his father.

Maia.note: Maia bears Mercury by Jupiter in the standard Greek-derived genealogy.
Vulcan's flamen sacrifices to Maia, and priestly prayers call her Maia Volcani.

Majestas.note: Personified Majesty remains beside Jupiter and protects his sceptre.

Malakbel.note: Palmyrene and Roman inscriptions style Malakbel as Sol Invictus Malachbel.

Mantus.note: Modern reconstructions make Mania his underworld consort without secure ancient evidence.

Marica.note: Faunus and the Laurentine nymph Marica are Latinus's parents.

Mars Ultor.note: Coin programs coordinated Mars's vengeance on the tyrant with Salus's promise of public salvation.

Marsyas.note: The chaste musician and healer accompanies Cybele during her grief-stricken wanderings.
Marsyas retrieves the flute Minerva invented, discarded, and cursed.

Mattiaca.note: Provincial dedications combine Diana with the locally bounded goddess Mattiaca.

Medocius Campesium.note: An obscure British dedication identifies Medocius Campesium with Mars.

Megaera.myth: Resistance to the Theban brothers’ duel
Megaera.note: Fides resists Megaera’s part in provoking fratricidal combat.

Melantho.note: Arachne’s tapestry depicts Neptune assuming dolphin form for Melantho.

Melicertes.note: Neptune transforms Melicertes into a sea-divinity after Venus intercedes.

Memalius.note: Cicero's fourth Vulcan is the son of Memalius.

Memnon.note: Memnon is the son of Aurora and Tithonus.

Memnon.myth: Aurora mourns Memnon and obtains memorial birds
Memnon.note: Aurora mourns Memnon and petitions Jupiter, who creates annually fighting Memnonides from his pyre.

Mena.note: Varro coordinates Mena's governance of menstruation with Juno Lucina's reproductive function.

Mendacium.note: Veritas walks after animation while her counterfeit Mendacium remains immobile.
Mendacium.source: Phaedrus, Appendix Perottina, Prometheus et Dolus

Mercury Heliopolitanus.note: Venus Heliopolitana appears with Mercury Heliopolitanus in a local imperial triad.

Minos.note: Hellenized Roman genealogy includes Minos among Jupiter’s heroic children.

Mogontia.note: Provincial dedications combine Diana with the locally bounded goddess Mogontia.

Mullo.note: The western Gaulish god Mullo was worshipped under the compound Mars Mullo.

Muse.note: Pindar jointly invokes the Muse and Alatheia to correct delayed praise.

Muta.note: Scholarly reconstruction sometimes identifies Muta with Mania through the Mater Larum tradition.

Myrrha.note: One reported tradition blames Venus for Myrrha's incest after neglected worship, though Ovid preserves alternatives.

Mā.note: Bellona's identity fused with the Cappadocian war goddess Mā.

Nantosuelta.note: Silvanus indirectly enters Nantosuelta's regional complex through his equation with her companion Sucellus.

Narcissus.myth: Narcissus persists as a garden flower
Narcissus.note: Flora includes the dead Narcissus among youths preserved as flowers.

Neleus.note: Neleus is Neptune’s child through Tyro in transferred Greek genealogy.

Nerio.note: Antiquarian comparison associates Bellona with Nerio, Mars's martial female partner.
Plautus and later antiquarians describe Nerio as Mars’s wife or partner.

Nessus.note: Hercules kills Nessus with a poisoned arrow after the centaur attacks Deianira.
Nessus’ poisoned blood later causes Hercules’ fatal burning and pyre.

Nethuns.note: The Etruscan water-god Nethuns is equated with Neptune.

Nicaea.note: Nicaea appears among Dionysus's loves in late Greek epic.

Night.myth: Circe invokes Night after transforming Picus
Night.note: Circe invokes Night while changing Picus’s companions after Picus becomes a bird.

Nile.note: Cicero's Vulcan-born Sun belongs to a genealogy in which Vulcan descends from Nile.

Niobe.note: Diana and Apollo punish Niobe by killing her daughters and sons.

Nixi.note: Alcmene jointly invokes Lucina and the collective birth gods called Nixi.

Numicius.note: Jupiter’s approval accompanies Numicius’s role in purifying and deifying Aeneas.

Ocelus.note: Western British evidence associates Ocelus or Vellaunus with Mars.

Odysseus.myth: Leucothea saves Odysseus from drowning with her veil
Odysseus.note: Ino-Leucothea gives Odysseus her veil and directs his escape from the sea.

Omphale.note: Faunus pursues Omphale but exchanged clothing leads him to Hercules.

Ophiuchus.note: Learned astral traditions identify the restored or deified healer with Ophiuchus.

Opis.note: Diana summons her attendant Opis and commands her to kill Arruns.

Orcus.note: Ennius calls Orcus another Latin name for Pluto, though later taxonomy distinguishes him.

Orestes.note: Orestes brings the Tauric Artemis image to Italy in Arician cult aetiology.

Orion.note: Eos takes Orion as a mortal lover before Artemis kills him at Ortygia.
Jupiter, Neptune, and Mercury jointly bring about Orion’s miraculous conception.
Some transferred Greek traditions make Orion a son of Neptune.

Orpheus.note: Proserpina and Pluto grant Orpheus a conditional release for Eurydice.

Ossa.note: Later mythography equates Roman Fama with the related Homeric figure Ossa.

Palaemon.note: Roman authors equate Portunus with the Greek harbour-god Palaemon, formerly Melicertes.

Pales.note: Caesius included a male Pales, Jupiter’s minister or steward, among them.

Pan Lycaeus.note: Carmenta directs the Arcadian settlers to establish a sanctuary dedicated to Pan Lycaeus.

Panacea.note: Panacea, the personification of universal remedy, belongs among his daughters.

Pandia.note: Selene bears Pandia by Zeus in the Homeric Hymn.

Pandora.note: Renaissance retellings recast Elpis as flower-bearing Spes remaining inside Pandora's vessel.

Panopea.myth: Sailors fulfill vows after reaching port
Panopea.note: Panopea and Melicertes are jointly invoked by sailors safely reaching port.

Pans.note: The Pans collectively pursue Pomona but fail to gain her.
The Pans and Silvanus are collectively listed as Pomona's pursuers.

Parcae.note: The Parcae and Ilithyia-Lucina appear jointly in Horace's official state hymn.

Paris.note: Paris judges Venus fairest after she promises him Helen.
Venus protects Paris during the Trojan War after winning his judgment.

Pavor.note: Pavor drives Mars's chariot and goads Fama to report truth or falsehood.

Pelias.note: Pelias is Neptune’s child through Tyro in transferred Greek genealogy.

Periphetes.note: Latin retellings sometimes substitute Vulcan as father of the robber Periphetes.

Perseus.note: Hellenized Roman genealogy makes Perseus Jupiter’s son by Danaë.

Phaedra.note: Venus causes Phaedra's destructive passion for her chaste stepson Hippolytus.

Phaenon.note: Greek astronomical tradition identifies Phaenon, the slow outer planet, with Saturn.

Phaethon.note: One Hesiodic genealogy makes Phaethon the child of Eos and Cephalus.
Luna watches in amazement while Phaethon loses control of Sol's chariot.
Sol is Phaethon's father through Clymene.
Bound by his oath, Sol reluctantly lets Phaethon drive his chariot for one day.

Philemon and Baucis.note: Jupiter rewards the hospitable couple with a temple and their final wish.
Jupiter grants their joint death, after which they become intertwined trees.

Philology.note: Mercury marries the personified Philology in an educational allegory attended by the liberal arts.

Phorcus.note: Phorcus appears with Neptune in the sculptural marine retinue.

Phēmē.note: Later mythography regularly presents Fama as the Roman equivalent of Greek Phēmē.

Picumnus.note: Ancient antiquarian and theological traditions conflate Picus with Picumnus, though modern scholarship distinguishes them.

Pilumnus.note: Pilumnus' pestle-sign helps repel Silvanus from the postpartum house.

Pirithous.note: Hercules attempts but in some accounts cannot rescue Pirithous.

Pistis.note: Greek authors use Pistis as the translation-equivalent of Roman Fides.

Pleione.note: Mercury descends from Pleione through her daughter Maia.

Podalirius.note: Podalirius, a physician and diagnostician at Troy, is his son.
Later cult images and dedications sometimes group Podalirius with his father.

Poseidon Hippios.note: Plutarch explains Consus and his horse rites through Horse Poseidon.

Poseidon Seisichthon.note: Some identified Consus with Earth-shaking Poseidon because his altar lay underground.

Postverta.myth: Paired Carmentes governing birth and temporal knowledge
Postverta.note: Postverta is Carmenta’s counterpart or divided aspect, governing reverse birth or knowledge of the future.

Prima.note: Plutarch preserves a disputed tradition making Prima a daughter of Romulus.

Prorsa.myth: Paired Carmentes governing birth and temporal knowledge
Prorsa.note: Prorsa is Carmenta’s counterpart or divided aspect, governing head-first birth or knowledge of the past.

Psyche.note: Cupid secretly marries Psyche; Jupiter later regularizes their divine marriage.
Cupid abandons Psyche after she secretly views him and wounds him with lamp oil.
Cupid removes Psyche’s deathlike sleep, returns it to the box, and awakens her.
Juno declines to shelter Psyche because she will not openly oppose Venus.
Mercury proclaims that the fugitive Psyche should be captured for Venus' promised reward.
Mercury summons the assembly where Psyche receives ambrosia, becomes immortal, and marries Cupid.
Jealous of Psyche's beauty, Venus persecutes her and imposes several impossible tasks.
Vulcan cooks the divine wedding banquet for Psyche and Cupid.

Pudor.note: Modesty and naked Truth jointly search for anyone equal to the dead Quintilius.

Pygmalion.note: Venus answers Pygmalion's festival prayer by animating his ivory woman.

Raven.note: The divine bird of Sol acts as messenger or intermediary between Sol and Mithras.

Remus.note: Fides and the reconciled Remus jointly give laws in Rome.
Later interpretation compared or identified a Lar Praestes with Remus.
Mars is the claimed divine father of Remus by Rhea Silvia.
As Romulus deified, Quirinus is the twin brother of Remus.
Virgil poetically reunites Quirinus and Remus as joint future lawgivers.

Repentance.note: Repentance turns tearfully toward Truth as Truth approaches the allegorical procession.

Rhadamanthus.note: Hellenized Roman genealogy includes Rhadamanthus among Jupiter’s heroic children.

Rhea Silvia.note: Rhea Silvia claims Mars fathered her twins; versions imply dream, seduction, or rape.
As Romulus deified, Quirinus inherits Rhea Silvia as his mother.

Roma.note: Libertas and Roma appear within the same republican coin issues and political visual programs.
The armed divine personification Roma accompanies Mars in the Augustan program.
Roma’s panel complemented a fecundity panel controversially identified as Pax.
Victoria crowns or accompanies the personified city and empire.

Roma Aeterna.note: Venus Felix and Roma Aeterna occupied adjoining back-to-back cellae in Hadrian's temple.

Romulus.note: Later interpretation compared or identified a Lar Praestes with Romulus.
The deified Romulus declares himself Quirinus and becomes Rome’s divine founder.

Romulus.myth: Roma and Romulus commemorate foundation and renewal
Romulus.note: Later coins place Roma and Romulus together in programs of foundation and renewal.

Rosmerta.note: Inscriptions and reliefs frequently pair Rosmerta with Mercury, although surviving evidence rarely explicitly calls them married.

Sabazios.note: Jupiter Sabazius combined Jupiter with Sabazios in varying cultic contexts.

Sabazius.note: The Thracian-Phrygian Sabazius was assimilated to Dionysus and Roman Liber.

Sagaritis.note: Cybele kills Sagaritis by destroying or wounding the tree sustaining her life.

Salacia.note: Roman cult and antiquarian theology name Salacia as Neptune’s partner or wife.

Samothracian Great Gods.note: Learned traditions linked the Penates with gods carried from Samothrace through Troy.

Satre.note: The Etruscan Satre may represent Saturn or a related deity; identification remains disputed.

Satyr.note: Visual traditions show Cupid or Eros-types struggling with a Satyr without a fixed narrative.

Satyrs.note: The Satyrs collectively pursue Pomona but fail to gain her.
The Satyrs and Silvanus are collectively listed as Pomona's pursuers.

Sea nymphs.note: Cybele's sacred-wood ships become sea nymphs under Jupiter's promised protection.

Seditio.note: Seditio resides among the personified forces inside Fama's cosmic house.

Semele.note: Semele bears Bacchus by Jupiter before dying in his divine fire.
Bacchus retrieves his mother and establishes her among the gods as Thyone.
Disguised as Beroe, Juno induces Semele to demand Jupiter’s lethal divine manifestation.
Juno’s deception causes Semele to be burned by Jupiter’s divine manifestation.
Jupiter becomes Semele’s lover and fathers Bacchus.
Bound by his promise, Jupiter appears in full power and burns Semele.
Ino is Semele's sister in the transferred Greek genealogy.
Through Melicertes, Portunus is Semele's nephew because Semele is Ino's sister.

Semo Sancus.note: Scholars hypothesized a relationship through Salus's isolated late title Semonia; no divine interaction is attested.

Semones.note: Invoked jointly with the Semones in the archaic agricultural hymn.

Shadrapha.note: A Punic-Latin bilingual dedication at Lepcis Magna directly equates Shadrapha with Liber.

Silenus.note: Silenus is Bacchus's tutor as well as his enduring companion.
Silenus accompanies Bacchus; his recovery from Midas prompts Bacchus to offer a gift.
The plural Fauns dance while Silenus performs his cosmic song.
Similar names and rustic iconography produced late and modern conflation with Silenus.

Silenus.myth: Priapus approaches Vesta at Cybele’s feast
Silenus.note: Silenus’s unattended ass awakens Vesta and frustrates Priapus.

Silvanae.note: Silvanus shares regional cult and reliefs with female Silvanae; their kinship is unstated.

Sime.note: Sime flanks Menrva in a securely inscribed Etruscan mirror scene of uncertain narrative.

Sirona.note: Mercury and Sirona occur together in some provincial domestic or sanctuary assemblages without a narrative.

Sol.note: Late theology identifies Liber as the nocturnal sun below the horizon.
Sol appears on the obverse of a related coin depicting Cloacina's shrine.

Sol.myth: Roma Aeterna joined with solar imagery
Sol.note: Solar symbolism makes Roma's duration coextensive with cosmic time.
The Senate coordinated honors to Sol with a proposed temple to Salus after Nero survived conspiracy.
Sol flanks Saturn on North-African stelae as an expression of celestial sovereignty.
Varro co-lists their altars among those supposedly vowed by Titus Tatius.

Sol.myth: Venus and Mars in the net
Sol.note: Sol discovers the adultery of Venus and Mars and informs Vulcan.

Somnus.note: Somnus contributes indirectly to Juno’s hostile program without receiving her direct command.

Soranus.note: Their neighboring cults share conflicting attribution of the Soracte fire-walk.

Stata Mater.note: Their cults complement each other in protecting Rome from urban fire.

Sterces.note: A rationalizing antiquarian genealogy makes the culture hero Sterces Picus’s father.

Steropes.note: Steropes labors under Vulcan on thunderbolts, Mars's chariot, and Minerva's aegis.

Suspicion.note: Truth approaches the allegorical scene opposing the deception encouraged by Suspicion.

Susurri.note: The collective Susurri inhabit Fama's house as whispers of doubtful authorship.

Symaethis.note: Faunus and the river-nymph Symaethis are Acis's parents.

Tacita.note: Ancient and modern scholarship has proposed Tacita as an identity of Mater Larum.

Telesphorus.note: Telesphorus appears as his subordinate son, embodying convalescence and completed recovery.
Telesphorus accompanies Aesculapius as a subordinate healing figure.

Tellus.note: Bellona is invoked before enemy lives are consigned to Tellus.
Tellus supplies soil and Ceres causes crops; they jointly receive agricultural prayer and sacrifice.
Cicero's philosophical theology alternatively identifies Ceres with the earth-goddess Tellus.
The Manes and Tellus jointly receive Decius and the enemy legions.
Scholars have proposed Tellus as an identity of Mater Larum and thus Mania.
Learned Roman theology explicitly identifies Vesta with Earth.

Terra.note: Terra produces Fama last in anger against the gods.
Terra receives Vulcan's semen and bears Erichthonius, whom Minerva subsequently raises.

Thalna.note: Thalna flanks Menrva in a securely inscribed Etruscan mirror scene of uncertain narrative.

The Fates.note: They restrain Pluto and determine or announce his marriage to Proserpina.

The Giants.note: Jupiter strikes the mountain-piling Giants with lightning.
Jupiter’s thunderbolts defeat and bury the Giants beneath mountains.

The Hours/Seasons.note: The Hours or Seasons scatter roses at Cupid and Psyche’s wedding.

The Titans.note: Jupiter and the younger gods defeat the Titans in the inherited succession war.

Theophane.note: Arachne’s tapestry depicts Neptune assuming ram form for Theophane.

Thesan.note: Thesan is comparatively equated with Aurora through shared dawn functions, not an ancient recorded meeting.
The Etruscan dawn goddess entered a reconstructed interpretive network linking Matuta and Leucothea.

Theseus.note: The brothers oppose Theseus and recover Helen after his abduction of her.

Theseus.myth: Rescue of Theseus from the underworld
Theseus.note: Hercules frees Theseus during his descent for Cerberus.

Tiber.note: Late aetiology associates Vertumnus or his sacrifices with diverting the river.

Tiberinus.myth: Leucothea arrives in the future Roman landscape
Tiberinus.note: The Tiber god receives or marks Leucothea's arrival in Latium.
The Calendar of 354's Tiberinalia may reflect displacement or assimilation of Portunus's festival.

Time.note: An unnamed old poet calls Truth the daughter of Time.

Timores.note: The collective Timores reside inside Fama's house and embody responses to rumour.

Tiresias.note: Tiresias adjudicates Juno and Jupiter’s dispute, ruling in Jupiter’s favor.
Juno blinds Tiresias after his judgment favors Jupiter.

Tisiphone.myth: Resistance to the Theban brothers’ duel
Tisiphone.note: Fides resists Tisiphone’s part in provoking fratricidal combat.
Juno commissions Tisiphone to destroy Athamas and Ino.

Titan.note: Ops secretly preserves children despite the succession agreement claimed by Titan.
Titan seizes and imprisons Ops with Saturn after discovering her deception.

Tithonus.note: Tithonus is Aurora's husband or enduring lover and father of her sons.
Aurora secures his immortality but neglects eternal youth, then tends his endless old age.
Later retellings say Aurora transformed aged Tithonus into a cicada or grasshopper.

Triptolemus.note: Ceres gives Triptolemus seed and a serpent-drawn chariot for his agricultural mission.
Ceres equips Triptolemus to teach agriculture throughout the world.
Ceres tends Triptolemus and attempts to immortalize him in fire before Metanira interrupts.

Trophonius.note: Learned catalogues identify or closely associate a subterranean Mercury with Trophonius.

Turnu.note: Some scholars tentatively identify the Etruscan Turnu as an equivalent of Eros or Cupid.

Turnus.note: Juno protects Turnus, creates a phantom Aeneas and prolongs his resistance.

Tyndareus.note: Tyndareus is one variant candidate for the dead person Aesculapius restored.
Castor is commonly Tyndareus' mortal son, while Pollux is Jupiter's.
Variant genealogies call both brothers sons of Tyndareus or Tyndarids.

Tyro.note: Neptune assumes the river Enipeus’s form to approach Tyro.

Upis.note: Cicero's third Diana, herself called Upis, is daughter of Upis.

Uṣas.note: Aurora and Uṣas are comparative cognate dawn goddesses without evidence of historical contact.

Vacuna.note: Older modern scholarship proposed identification, but decisive ancient evidence is absent.

Valetudo.note: Salus and Valetudo occupy opposite coin faces, associating but possibly distinguishing civic safety and bodily health.

Veltune.note: The Etruscan mirror deity is sometimes equated with Vertumnus, though the connection remains disputed.

Venilia.note: One tradition makes Janus and Venilia co-parents of Canens.
Varro’s system attaches Venilia to Neptune as incoming wave or second consort.
Venilia.source: Varro through Augustine, City of God 7.22

Vica Pota.note: Ancient antiquarians assimilated Vica Pota to Victoria, though original identity is unproved.

Victory.note: Carmenta’s Arcadian settlers establish Victory’s precinct during the settlement of Pallantium.
Imperial imagery associates Iuventa Imperii with an emperor holding Victory’s statuette.

Virbius.myth: Virbius attempts to console grieving Egeria
Virbius.note: Virbius recounts his death and restoration but cannot relieve Egeria’s grief.
Virgil places Virbius in Egeria’s groves without narrating direct interaction.

Virtus.note: Bellona and Virtus appear jointly in a list of martial deities.
Imperial evidence names Dea Virtus Bellona and equates Virtus with Bellona.
Plutarch stages Fortune and Virtue as competing explanations for Rome’s imperial greatness.

Voluptas.note: Voluptas is the daughter born from Cupid and Psyche’s union.

YHWH.note: Some Greco-Roman writers polemically associated the Jewish deity and Sabbath with Saturn.

Zelos.note: Victoria is called his sister only through identification with Nike.
Zelos.date: late eighth or early seventh century BCE

daimōn.note: Imperial Platonism equates the personal Genius with a Greek daemon or embodied soul.

deified emperors.note: Victoria shares imperial state sacrificial lists with deified emperors.

fifty daughters.note: Elean tradition makes Luna and Endymion parents of fifty daughters.

guardian angel.note: Late antique and medieval thought compared guardian angels with Genii without establishing direct identity.

imperial numen.note: A dedication jointly honors the imperial numen and Mercurius Dumiatis.

local nymphs.note: The local nymphs urge the grieving Egeria to moderate her lamentation.

the Aloadae.note: The Aloadae are Neptune’s children through Iphimedia in transferred Greek genealogy.

the Camenae.note: The Camenae and Vertumnus share a calendrical commemoration date.

the Campestres.note: Victoria and the Campestres occur within one provincial military dedication.

the Fates.note: Plutarch reports an interpretation identifying Carmenta as one of the Fates.

the Furies.myth: Resistance to the Theban brothers’ duel
the Furies.note: Fides and Pietas oppose the Furies but are overcome.

the Giants.note: Minerva fights the Giants as a defender of divine cosmic order.
As young Jupiter, Vediovis precedes the war when the Giants attacked heaven.

the Heliades.note: The Heliades, including Phaethusa and Lampetia, are daughters of Sol.
Sol's daughters mourn their brother Phaethon and are transformed into poplars.

the Larvae.note: Lexicographical tradition calls Mania the mother of the frightening Larvae.
the Larvae.source: Festus and Paulus, De verborum significatu

the Larvae.note: A variant lexicographical tradition calls Mania the Larvae's grandmother.
the Larvae.source: Festus and Paulus, De verborum significatu

the Maenads.myth: Maenads threaten Leucothea near the Ara Maxima
the Maenads.note: Maenads attack or threaten Leucothea during her arrival in Latium.

the Nile.note: Arnobius includes a secret-named Egyptian Mercury born from the Nile.
Cicero's Egyptian Vulcan, identified as Phthas, is the Nile's son.

the Novensides.note: Varro lists Feronia and the Novensides among Sabine-derived divinities.

the Roman people.note: Mars is politically represented as Rome’s ancestor through his son Romulus.

the Seasons.note: The Seasons frame Dionysus's cosmic triumph in imperial funerary iconography.

the Titans.note: The Titans lure, kill, dismember, cook, and consume the child Dionysus.
Titan's sons assist in seizing and imprisoning Ops and Saturn.

the goddess of Eryx.note: Romans identified Eryx's Sicilian goddess as Venus Erycina.

the gods.note: Jupiter convenes divine councils and announces decisions concerning cosmic and mortal affairs.

the household Genius.note: Household paintings frequently place the Genius between paired Lares.

the river Numicius.note: At Venus's request, Numicius washes Aeneas's mortal elements away before apotheosis.

the river gods.note: Neptune summons the river gods and orders them to release their waters.

the stars.note: Eos and Astraeus are parents of the stars.
